newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russian economic guru is liberal father-figure.
newsitem.headline: New Russian economic guru is liberal father-figure.

text.p: Russia's new government has a distinctly youthful look, with many of its top ministers under 50. But Yevgeny Yasin, named on Wednesday to coordinate economic reforms behind the scenes, is very much of an older generation.

At 62, the diminutive economics professor is old enough to be the father of Anatoly Chubais, 41, and Boris Nemtsov, 37, the two first deputy prime ministers charged with putting an end to Russia's profound economic malaise.

Indeed, Kremlin officials say it is as a father-figure that many of the young generation of liberals view Yasin, who first established his reformist credentials in the perestroika era under Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.
His new role appears to confirm his position as a backroom guide for the new-look cabinet, which President Boris Yeltsin hopes can rescue market reforms from inertia and corruption.
Replaced as economy minister earlier this month by his former deputy Yakov Urinson, Yasin was appointed minister without portfolio on Wednesday by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
"Yevgeny Yasin is now a minister," Chernomyrdin said. "He will deal with economic questions, including coordinating work on our programmes, reviewing them and analysing them."

Yasin, whose bushy brow and bald pate make him instantly recognisable in a cabinet of younger men, has played a key role in negotiations with international financial organisations and with the Group of Seven industrialised countries.

He was one of the authors of the radical 500 Days programme presented to Gorbachev in 1990 as a shock therapy designed to transform the Soviet Union from communism to capitalism. Gorbachev baulked but the authors, who included liberal leader Grigory Yavlinsky, maintained their profile under Yeltsin.
Yasin went on to be economics director of the Union of Entrepreneurs and Industrialists and worked in Yeltsin's Kremlin administration before being named economy minister in 1994.
For the 15 years before 1989, Yasin was a senior economist studying central planning in the Soviet system.
Born in the Ukrainian Black Sea city of Odessa, he worked first as a bridge-building engineer before going on to study economics in Moscow. His wife and daughter are also economists.
